vignette: He stands at the window of his study, watching the rain streak the glass. At forty-nine, his hands still bear the calluses of years spent gripping rifle stocks and handling heavy gear, but his life now revolves around zoning ordinances, infrastructure budgets, and the quiet rhythm of municipal governance. The memories that brought him to this therapist’s office began in a sun-bleached valley three decades ago. He was twenty when the mortar round hit his convoy. The sound still lives in his teeth—a sharp, metallic ring that drowns out his wife’s voice when she calls him for dinner. He remembers the dust, the screaming, the way the world narrowed to a tunnel of smoke and broken radio static. When the dust settled, he walked away, but something inside him fractured. It never quite reassembled. In the years since, he learned to bury the fracture beneath a life of rigid routine. He ran for the City Council because the chamber offered structure he could control. Seats arranged in perfect arcs, agendas typed in advance, debate timed to the second. He tells himself it is civic duty, but the truth is quieter. He needs to know what comes next. When constituents speak too quickly or when the microphone feedback whines, his pulse jumps to his throat. He has developed a practiced stillness for public appearance, but behind his desk, he sorts through mail with military precision, checking envelopes twice for hidden threats that do not exist. He carries the quiet stoicism of his European ancestry, but it is no longer enough to shield him from the weight of his own nervous system. At home, his marriage survives on careful navigation. His wife knows not to tap his shoulder unexpectedly. She knows the silence that falls over him when fireworks crackle in the distance, or when a garbage truck backfires on their street. He does not tell her he stays awake until 3 a.m., staring at the ceiling, replaying the convoy route in his head, calculating which vehicle would have taken the hit differently. He stops taking the scenic route to the grocery store, avoiding underpasses because the rumble of tires on concrete feels like approaching engines. He deletes weather maps from his phone; sudden changes in the sky trigger a cold sweat that leaves him trembling in the pantry. He tells himself he is just being cautious, but his body has forgotten how to rest. Tuesday council sessions remain his anchor and his test. He sits in the third row, always facing the door, his posture rigid. When a developer shouts over the mayor, the old wiring in his spine fires. His jaw locks. His breath becomes shallow. He forces himself to take notes, the pen moving in tight, deliberate circles, grounding him in the room. He tells himself the arguments are just noise, but his body disagrees. He has learned to request breaks when the volume climbs too high, citing “migraines,” which is not entirely a lie. The pressure behind his eyes mirrors the pressure in his chest. He votes with conviction. He smiles when necessary. He shakes hands with constituents who praise his reliability, noting how he always knows the exit routes in every municipal building. Yet, when the chamber lights dim and the gavel strikes, he still flinches, just slightly, at the sudden crack of authority. The work demands compromise, but compromise requires surrendering control, and he has not mastered that skill since the valley. He leaves every session feeling drained, as if he has been running, not sitting. On weekends, he walks the dog along the river path. He likes the water because it moves steadily, predictably. He watches the couples strolling past, some laughing, some arguing, and feels a strange distance, as if he is observing them through thick glass. He loves his wife. He tries to reach her, to laugh at her jokes, to be present, but part of him remains parked in that valley, waiting for orders that never come. He attends committee meetings with a clipboard and a calm voice. He signs ordinances. He pays his taxes. He lives in the quiet, controlled space between survival and living, waiting for the dust to finally settle.
